# Introduction

The way in which children and youths come to understand who succeeds in society and why is a relevant aspect of the socialization process [@mijs_unfulfillable_2016; @resh_sense_2014]. Schools are important actors in this regard, as they use grading, tracking, and selection to apply meritocratic criteria based primarily on individual talent and effort [@traini_stratification_2022; @darnon_where_2018]. This early exposure to meritocratic principles in the "impressionable years" [@krosnick_aging_1989] shapes students' understanding of fairness, social mobility, and social hierarchies. At the same time, schools are environments where students encounter evidence that outcomes are shaped by factors other than meritocratic ones, such as family background, social connections, and structural advantages usually associated with privilege [@bourdieu_reproduction_1990; @goudeau_hidden_2017a; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. These background attributes can be considered privileges due to heritage-based advantages over which people have no control, unlike effort. Yet, few studies have explored how students conceive meritocracy and to what extent such conceptions challenge the role of privilege in society.

Although meritocracy is often treated as a single dimension, mostly related to individual effort, the literature increasingly suggests that it is a multidimensional construct. On the one hand, this refers to the distinction between perceptions of how meritocracy operates in society ("what is") and preferences about how it should operate ("what ought to be") [@duru-bellat_whos_2012; @castillo_multidimensional_2023]. On the other hand, meritocratic beliefs can be distinguished from privilege-based beliefs, which emphasize the role of family wealth and social connections in shaping rewards in society [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. A multidimensional approach should therefore incorporate perceptions and preferences about both meritocratic and privilege-based explanations of social outcomes, in line with Khan's [-@khan_privilege_2013] call to analyze meritocracy together with privilege.

Previous research has shown that privilege and meritocratic beliefs represent different and not necessarily opposite dimensions, therefore they can coexist in people's minds [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025; @fan_disillusionment_2026]. This means, for instance, that someone could believe that society rewards talent and effort while also acknowledging that family wealth and social connections play (or should play) a role in shaping outcomes. However, attempts to study these beliefs have been limited by the lack of instruments that capture their multidimensionality and by the absence of longitudinal studies that examine how these beliefs evolve over time. We contribute to this agenda by applying a multidimensional model to measure meritocratic and privilege beliefs in a sample of Chilean students and by examining the stability and measurement equivalence of these beliefs across school stages and over time. We argue that meritocratic and privilege beliefs can be distinguished even at an early school age, with a structure similar to that found among adults [@castillo_multidimensional_2023]; that they are not two ends of the same continuum but can coexist in students' minds; and that they are not static but evolve as students accumulate experience and exposure to different social contexts.

We draw on a two-wave panel of Chilean students in primary and secondary school cohorts. Chile's educational system combines high stratification, market-based competition, and explicit meritocratic discourse in school culture [@castillo_socialization_2024; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2013], alongside persistent socioeconomic inequality and a deep marketization of social welfare [@ferre_welfare_2023; @madariaga_three_2020], features shared by many Latin American countries and increasingly present in European and East Asian systems [@busemeyer_skills_2014; @gingrich_making_2011]. This makes Chile a productive case for studying how students internalize, question, or reconcile meritocratic ideals with the reality of privilege, although whether the dimensional structure and longitudinal patterns identified here hold in other highly stratified educational contexts remains to be tested.


The research questions guiding this study are as follows:

(1) Are school-aged students able to distinguish between meritocratic and privilege-based principles, as well as between perceptions ("what is") and preferences ("what should be")?

(2) Are meritocratic beliefs undermined (i.e., negatively associated) by beliefs about privilege, or could they coexist in students' minds?

(3) Are these dimensions stable over time and across school stages?
